name: FaceTune / AI eye whitening

lead: Photo apps such as FaceTune offer tools to whiten the sclera and brighten the iris in pictures, giving eyes a brighter, more vivid look in photos.

The software selects the eye region, sometimes using AI segmentation, and increases brightness or saturation. The edit changes the photograph only, not your actual eyes, and no research on eye-whitening edits was found.

paras: People apply the edit in a photo app after taking a picture, usually with a light touch, before posting or sharing. Results appear instantly in the edited image.
No physical risks. Critics of heavy retouching in general raise concerns about unrealistic image standards, though no study specific to eye whitening was found.

angle.text: FaceTune and similar apps whiten the sclera and brighten the iris in a photo, making eyes look brighter and more vivid in the picture. The edit is instant and changes the image only.

lead: FaceTune and similar photo-editing apps let users retouch selfies, including whitening the sclera (the white of the eye), brightening the iris and removing redness. Newer AI-based editors apply the same adjustments automatically, often through a one-tap enhance or beauty feature. People use eye whitening to make their eyes look brighter, clearer and more rested in photos and profile pictures, one of the quickest ways to change how a face reads on screen.

Facetune was made by the Israeli company Lightricks and launched in March 2013 as a paid app. Its original features included smoothing skin, whitening teeth, reshaping faces, sharpening the area around the eyes and adjusting lighting; later versions added one-tap fixes, eye and facial feature refinement and, from 2022, AI-based enhancement.[1] Wikipedia reports it was named to Apple's Best of 2013 list, was Apple's most-downloaded paid app in 2017 and had been downloaded over 200 million times by 2023.[1]

In looksmaxxing discussion the technique comes up mainly around photo presentation, such as dating profiles and social media, alongside lighting, angle and lens choices that affect how a face is captured. Critics quoted by Wikipedia argue that such apps can distort self-image and set unrealistic beauty standards, and a 2020 study is cited as linking selfie-editing apps to greater desire for cosmetic surgery.[1]
infobox: FaceTune and other retouching or AI beauty apps
Sclera whitening, iris brightening, redness reduction

paras: Retouching apps provide a brush or automatic tool that lightens the whites of the eyes and can sharpen or saturate the iris. AI features detect the eye region automatically and apply the adjustment without manual masking. Many also offer related edits such as teeth whitening, blemish removal and skin smoothing.
The Wikipedia Facetune article describes the app's eye-area tools as part of a wider set of retouching features that also cover blemish and wrinkle removal, teeth whitening and relighting.[1]

Users describe applying subtle whitening and brightening to profile and dating photos so that the eyes look more awake. Discussion of the technique tends to sit with other presentation choices such as lighting, camera distance and angle, which also change how the eye area appears.

Commentators on social media have also noted that heavily edited photos can look different from a person in real life, and some users prefer light adjustments so that images stay close to their appearance.

The edit changes only the image. People who want a brighter appearance of the eyes in person commonly discuss separate approaches such as sleep, hydration, lubricating or redness-relieving eye drops, and eyewear, which are covered in their own entries.

Retouching in general is discussed in terms of body image: Wikipedia notes that filters in Instagram, TikTok and Facetune let users reshape their own images and that young people are exposed to unrealistic beauty ideals, and describes disclosure rules such as France's 2015 retouching law and Norway's 2021 law on labeling digitally altered bodies in advertising.[2] Critics of selfie-editing apps raise catfishing and body dysmorphia concerns, and the term Snapchat dysmorphia describes people seeking surgery to resemble filtered selves.[1]

timeline.event: Lightricks launches Facetune as a paid app and it is named to Apple's Best of 2013 list.[1]
